extracted.intended_audience: general readers, writers, comedians, and linguists interested in puns/wordplay
extracted.subtask_description: Taxonomy and practical guidance for creating and using puns: definitions, types (homophonic, homographic, homonymic, compounded, recursive, visual, paronomastic, metonymic, syllepsis, antanaclasis, morphological/graphological), and considerations for rhetorical, design, and media uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a pun / paronomasia
rubrics_metrics.description: A pun (also known as a paronomasia) is a form of word play that exploits multiple meanings of a term, or of similar-sounding words, for an intended humorous or rhetorical effect. These ambiguities can arise from the intentional use of homophonic, homographic, metonymic, or figurative language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish puns from malapropisms (a malapropism is an incorrect variation on a correct expression; a pun involves expressions with multiple correct or reasonable interpretations). Recognize that puns are often language- and culture-specific and may function as in-jokes or idiomatic constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Homophonic pun
rubrics_metrics.description: A homophonic pun is one that uses word pairs which sound alike (homophones) but are not synonymous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'atheism is a non-prophet institution' (prophet/profit); 'to keep the Russians in Czech' (check/Czech). Note: puns often use similar, not identical, sounds (peas/peace). Walter Redfern: 'To pun is to treat homonyms as synonyms.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Homographic (heteronymic) pun
rubrics_metrics.description: A homographic pun exploits words that are spelled the same (homographs) but possess different meanings and sounds; they rely on sight more than hearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sometimes called heteronymic puns. Often rely on unusual sentence construction; may not make sense when interpreted outside context. Example: 'You can tune a guitar, but you can't tuna fish. Unless of course, you play bass.' (combines homophonic and homographic elements).

rubrics_metrics.name: Homonymic pun
rubrics_metrics.description: Homonymic puns arise from the exploitation of words that are both homographs and homophones (same spelling and sound) used with different meanings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Being in politics is just like playing golf: you are trapped in one bad lie after another' (lie = untruth / lie = position). Homonymic puns may be polysemic (related meanings) or treated as separate lemmata by lexicographers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compound pun
rubrics_metrics.description: A compound pun is a statement that contains two or more puns, where the wordplay of the whole cannot be reduced to the separate puns working individually.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example Richard Whately: multiple layered puns within one passage. Compound puns may also combine phrases that share a word (e.g., Möbius strip club). They can be complex and dense—use carefully to avoid confusing the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recursive pun
rubrics_metrics.description: A recursive pun is one in which the second aspect of a pun relies on the understanding of an element in the first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'π is only half a pie' (π radians = 180°) and 'Infinity is not in finity'. The second element presupposes comprehension of the first; these often reward more knowledgeable audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual pun
rubrics_metrics.description: A visual pun replaces one or more aspects of the pun with a picture or exploits visual similarity (shape) rather than phonetic similarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in logos, heraldry (canting arms), cartoons, gable stones, and non-phonetic writing systems (e.g., Chinese character-shape puns). Example: US Air Force 148th Fighter Squadron emblem literally depicting 'Kickin' Ass.' Also used in games like 4 Pics 1 Word.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paronomastic puns (manipulation of idioms/phrases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Paronomasia is the formal term for punning; paronomastic puns manipulate well-known idioms, proverbs, or phrases to deliver a punned twist, often using the classic setup–punchline joke structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frequently used in advertising, comedy, and literature to provide clever memorable messages. Example: 'I used to be a baker, but I couldn't make enough dough' (dough = bread mixture / money). Good paronomasia leverages familiarity with the original phrase.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metonymic pun
rubrics_metrics.description: Metonymic puns exploit the metonymic relationship between words—using one term to represent something closely associated with it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example headline-like pun: 'The White House loses its balance' (White House = U.S. government; balance = physical or fiscal). These puns rely on conceptual links and can create layered interpretations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sylleptic / heteronymic (syllepsis) pun
rubrics_metrics.description: Syllepsis is a form of punning where a single word simultaneously affects the rest of the sentence while changing meaning across its uses (literal and metaphorical senses at once).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'She lowered her standards by raising her glass, her courage, her eyes and his hopes.' The word applies differently to each coordinate—this can create a chain of linked puns and rhetorical effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antanaclasis
rubrics_metrics.description: Antanaclasis is a type of pun where a single word or phrase is repeated but the meaning changes each time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example Benjamin Franklin: 'We must, indeed, all hang together or, most assuredly, we shall all hang separately.' First 'hang' = stick together; second 'hang' = be executed. Repetition with shifting meaning creates surprise and wit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graphological / morphological / other forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Other pun forms include graphological (visual) puns, morphological puns (portmanteaux), rebracketing, and self-referential puns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: rebracketing 'distressed' as 'dis-tressed'; portmanteaux; the self-referential 'I entered ten puns...but no pun in ten did' (no pun intended). These techniques broaden the toolkit beyond phonetics and orthography.

rubrics_metrics.name: Puns as comedy device (punchlines and parodies)
rubrics_metrics.description: Puns are a common source of humour in jokes and comedy shows, often used in punchlines and in titles of parodies to signal the target of parody immediately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They can function as feghoots (punch-line-dependent jokes). Useful for quick laughs and signalling parody, but may be regarded as low-brow by some audiences—consider context and audience taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Puns as literary device
rubrics_metrics.description: Puns have been used as standard poetic and literary devices, sometimes non-humorously, to introduce ambiguity and multiple meanings into serious or refined texts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notable practitioners include Shakespeare, Donne, Joyce, Nabokov. Historically, puns could indicate literary refinement; they may be used in 'seemingly inappropriate' serious scenes to add depth rather than mere comic relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetorical use of puns
rubrics_metrics.description: Puns can function as a rhetorical device and persuasive instrument when used responsibly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Major difficulty: audiences with different backgrounds may interpret a pun very differently, potentially detracting from the intended message. Use caution when stakes are high; ensure the audience can access the intended ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design/branding use (attention-getting / mnemonic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Paronomasia is used for its attention-getting or mnemonic qualities in titles, place names, character names, and advertising slogans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common in shop and restaurant names, product slogans, and fictional character names. Multilingual and cultural factors can affect comprehension; puns can be highly effective for memorability but risk misunderstanding if audience lacks needed language/cultural knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media and headline use
rubrics_metrics.description: Paronomasia has a strong presence in media, especially headlines, where catchiness is valued to draw readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Headline puns (e.g., 'Headless Body in Topless Bar') are attention-grabbing but can be perceived as tasteless or trivializing. Editors use paronomasia for rapid impact—be aware of ethical and tonal consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confusion and overlap with related devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Puns overlap with other literary techniques (double entendre, paraprosdokian, syllepsis, eggcorns, antanaclasis, polyptoton) and can be confused with them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate intentionally: a double entendre often alludes to a second meaning not contained in the phrase itself; homographic puns may resemble antanaclasis; homophonic puns may resemble polyptoton. Puns can also function as mnemonic devices. Linguists sometimes propose neologisms to reduce ambiguity caused by puns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural, historical, and cross-linguistic considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Punning has a long global history (ancient Egypt, Mesopotamia, China, Hebrew Bible, Maya hieroglyphs, Japan's dajare, Tamil slesha, Telugu slesha) and many puns are language- or culture-specific.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bilingual or multilingual puns require audience knowledge of more than one language. Historical and cultural contexts affect whether puns function as humor, rhetoric, or poetic device. When creating puns for diverse audiences, account for linguistic accessibility and potential loss of wordplay in translation.
